title_original: Previously Unknown Canaletto Drawing Reemerges After Centuries
excerpt_original: The work is crossing the auction block in the U.K., where it is estimated to fetch $79,000.

blocks.text: Canaletto may be famed for his sweeping vistas of Venice and London, but the artist himself rather fancied his capricci , works composed of imagined buildings, ruins, and scenery. One of these, a previously unknown drawing, is landing on the auction block at Mallams in Oxford, the U.K. on October 21, carrying an estimate of £40,000 to £60,000 ($53,000 to $79,000).

The pen and brown ink drawing depicts a crumbling arcade invaded by greenery rising above a rickety bridge. A boatman emerges from a dilapidated archway. In the foreground, Canaletto scatters the detritus of an abandoned wheel and a wooden plank on a bank of silt. Dated to 1746 to 1755, the latter portion of Canaletto’s stint in England, it’s a romantic vision of past grandeur, one an inscription on the back indicates the artist gave as a gift.
The work was likely acquired by Charles Burney , the distinguished Georgian composer and music historian, in the late 18th century and has been passed down through his family to the present day.

“His capriccio pictures form a small portion of Canaletto’s oeuvre and this drawing includes many elements typical of this genre: monumental architectural structures, ruins, water, and groups of figures, known as staffage,” the art historian John Rolfe said over email. “They show brilliant observation, an eye for detail, but also imagination, fantasy, and drama.”

Authenticated by Canaletto expert Charles Beddington , the previously unrecorded sheet probably served as a preparatory drawing that was shown to a patron ahead of a related painting. That work last appeared at Christie’s London in 1995 where it sold for £380,000 (then $577,000).

blocks.alt: a close up of the Canaletto work with strong shadows and a boatman.

blocks.text: Detail of the Canaletto capriccio. Photo: courtesy Mallams.

Though the capriccio emerged in the 17th century, Canaletto was one of the first artists to develop the genre fully as a major component of his practice. Beginning in the late 1730s, it allowed him to blend familiar architectures with those of his imagination. As to why Canaletto began painting capricci , Rolfe suggested several possibilities: a response to the decline in tourism to Venice during the continental wars, a response to a new cult of ruins, or a continuation of the theatrical work he had done for his father, a stage designer.

According to the Artnet Price Database , the record for a Canaletto capriccio at auction is the £2.2 million (then $3.3 million) paid for A Capriccio of the Scuola di San Marco, Venice, from the Palazzo Grifalconi-Loredan (1750s) at Christie’s London in 1994.

Two of Canaletto’s three highest auction prices have come in the past two years. In July 2025, Venice, the Return of the Bucintoro on Ascension Day set the artist’s record, selling for £32 million ($44 million) at Christie’s London. This February, a vertical format painting focused on the same theme sold for $30.5 million.

More broadly, Canaletto’s market has been solid, rather than spectacular in recent years. Over the past three years, the average price for his works has been $64,500, with 40 percent of lots selling above their high estimates. From 2019 to 2023, the average price was $536,321 with a similar share of lots exceeding their high estimates.
